name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,618

clue.text: Prime Minister has sex appeal in part

blocks.note: PT is the standard abbreviation for part
'it' is old slang for sex appeal, as in the It girl

explanation.surface: A gossipy line about a Prime Minister with a bit of charisma.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal comes from 1920s slang and is a setters' favourite. PITT is either William Pitt, father or son, both Prime Ministers of Great Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: William Pitt the Elder and the Younger both led British governments, so the surname names a premier.

clue.text: Sanctimonious learner caught formidable fish

blocks.note: pi is informal British for piously self-righteous
L for learner, from the L-plates on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A preachy novice angler lands a fearsome catch.
explanation.walkthrough: PI (short for pious) is a British schoolboy word for sanctimonious, and C for caught comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilchard is a small oily sea creature of the herring family, often sold tinned.

clue.text: Flower from wood miles away

explanation.surface: A bloom found in a forest far from anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword trick: read it as flow-er, something that flows, a river. The Tiber runs through Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: In crosswordese a flower is anything that flows, so a river such as Rome's qualifies.

clue.text: Matthew perhaps sliced bananas, holding one with pressure

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Someone called Matthew chopping fruit, perhaps for breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sliced bananas' reads as a fruit salad but 'bananas' is the anagram signal. 'Perhaps' warns that Matthew is only one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Matthew the tax collector was one of the twelve apostles, the followers of Jesus.

clue.text: Narrow strip of land connecting areas is therefore restricting motorway

definitions.text: Narrow strip of land connecting areas

blocks.note: M for motorway, as in the M1

explanation.surface: A planning note about a motorway squeezed along a thin neck of land.
explanation.walkthrough: British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on, which is why M stands for motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: An isthmus is a thin neck of ground with sea on each side, joining two larger landmasses, like Panama.

clue.text: New Tory campaign he's filming

indicators.note: a new version of the letters means rearranging them

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician shooting a campaign video.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking the fodder to the definition. A single-word definition beside a fourteen-letter answer signals a long anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinematography is the art and craft of motion-picture camera work, which is what shooting a movie involves.

clue.text: Head teacher's rule read aloud

blocks.note: a principle is a rule, and it is pronounced the same as its twin

explanation.surface: A headteacher reading out the school rules at assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: The two spellings are a famous confusion: principle is the rule, principal the person in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A principal is the person in charge of a school or college, a synonym common in America.

clue.text: Woman put on new uniform

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece put on another sits above it

explanation.surface: A woman changes into a fresh uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like a noun, something to wear, but it is the adjective: the same all through.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform as an adjective means consistent and regular throughout, which is one sense of the answer.

clue.text: Captain may need this gun with plan to purchase one

blocks.note: an automatic is a self-loading gun

explanation.surface: A captain planning to buy a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: The captain is an airline pilot, not a soldier or ship's master, and the gun is only there to supply the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft captain relies on the autopilot system to fly the plane hands-free on long stretches.

clue.text: Drop trousers I had split

indicators.note: as a verb, to trouser is to pocket

blocks.note: a dive is a sudden drop

explanation.surface: An embarrassing moment where someone's trousers fall down and tear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' is the verb here: to trouser money is British slang for pocketing it.
explanation.definitionFit: To split something is to separate it into parts, a direct synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Requiring lots of hands to rub in Vaseline all over the place

indicators.note: things scattered everywhere are out of order, so the letters get rearranged

explanation.surface: A messy job smearing petroleum jelly everywhere, needing many helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' means workers, as in farmhands, rather than the hands doing the rubbing in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A job needing many workers relies heavily on human effort, which is what the compound adjective describes.

clue.text: Hurt leg - I knocked over Greek character's organ

indicators.note: something knocked over lies the other way round

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side
mu is the Greek letter M

explanation.surface: Someone hurts a leg knocking over a Greek person's musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: ON for leg is cricket: the leg side of the field is also the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonium is a small keyboard instrument that pumps air through reeds, a type of reed organ.

clue.text: Minute hole in one weapon

blocks.note: a hole in one at golf is an ace

explanation.surface: A tiny puncture in a single weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' reads as tiny (my-NEWT) but is the unit of time (MIN-it), abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: A mace is a heavy club with a spiked or flanged head, used in medieval combat.

clue.text: Strain from boy holding rake? On the contrary

blocks.note: a roué is a rake, a dissolute man

explanation.surface: A boy straining while carrying a garden rake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' reverses the stated instruction: instead of the boy holding the rake, the rake (a libertine, not a garden tool) holds the boy.
explanation.definitionFit: In music a roulade is a rapid run of notes sung to one syllable, and a strain is a musical passage.

clue.text: Take reins off a horse? Nun's ordered nothing's removed

indicators.note: nothing is the round letter shaped like zero
putting things in order means rearranging them

explanation.surface: A nun at a stable, ordering someone to untack a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing' is O, taken from 'a horse' before the anagram. The question mark after 'horse' disguises that 'a horse' is fodder, not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To take the tack and straps off a draught animal is to release it from its gear.

clue.text: Legs it upstairs, welcoming part of a keep-fit routine?

explanation.surface: Someone dashing up the stairs as part of their exercise routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legs it' is British slang for runs off, which makes the surface sound like exercise while the letters run across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Sit-ups are abdominal exercises done lying down and raising the torso, a staple of any workout.

clue.text: Hairy fly in red cordial

indicators.note: hairy means wild or dicey, so the letters that follow run wild

explanation.surface: An insect drowning in a glass of red fruit drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cordial' pretends to be the drink, as British cordial is a fruit syrup diluted with water; here it is the adjective, meaning warm.
explanation.definitionFit: Cordial as an adjective means warm and genial in manner, a synonym for being amicable.

clue.text: 1960s model ignoring fashion for seafood

explanation.surface: A sixties supermodel who shunned fashion for a seafood diet.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Shrimpton was a leading 1960s British model, nicknamed The Shrimp. TON is an old word for fashion, as in 'bon ton'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrimps are small shellfish eaten widely, a common example of food from the sea.

clue.text: Set of audio files - quiet with almost strange pitch

blocks.note: to pitch is to throw, to cast

explanation.surface: Recordings that are soft but have an odd tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' belongs to the sound of the surface, but here it is the verb to throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A podcast is an episodic series of digital recordings released for download or streaming.

clue.text: Soldier's gun returned by a king

blocks.note: a Luger is a German pistol

explanation.surface: A soldier's weapon handed back to a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay rather than making a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular is a professional soldier in a standing army, as opposed to a reservist.

clue.text: River ultimately where small fish live

blocks.note: the ide is a freshwater fish, a crossword staple

explanation.surface: A note on the river habitat of little fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River ultimately' looks like a pair, but 'ultimately' works on 'where', not on 'River'.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to have your home there, a formal synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Support for Portugal

blocks.note: P is Portugal's international vehicle registration

explanation.surface: Backing a football or national team, Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support for Portugal' reads as cheering a team; 'Support' is the definition and 'for' gives the first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A prop is a pole or beam holding something up, and also a verb for bolstering.

clue.text: Is soldier for example retreating after duke's ridicule?

blocks.note: D = duke, as in peerage abbreviations

explanation.surface: Asking whether a soldier is falling back under an aristocrat's mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After duke's' puts the other pieces after D; the 's is possessive in the surface but only a join in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To disparage is to belittle or speak scornfully of someone, much like mocking them.

clue.text: Beer crate oddly dropped on one's toes

blocks.note: cRaTe with its 1st, 3rd and 5th letters gone

explanation.surface: A crate of beer falling on someone's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On one's toes' looks like where the crate lands; it is an idiom for watchful and ready.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on your toes is an idiom for being watchful and ready to react quickly.

clue.text: Bird taking top off for creep

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, which is taken away

explanation.surface: A bird doffing its cap to a lowlife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creep' tempts as a noun, an unpleasant person, but it is the verb: to move slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: To inch forward is to move very slowly by small degrees, as creeping does.

clue.text: New torn leather, dad? Need this?

definitions.text: New torn leather, dad? Need this?

indicators.note: something torn is ripped apart, so the fodder words are pulled to pieces and remade

explanation.surface: A child telling their father his brand-new leather has ripped and asking if he needs a repair kit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the setter expects you to see what is required to mend a tear. 'New' is not the anagram signal but gives N.
explanation.definitionFit: Stitching up a rip in leather requires a sewing tool and a length of cotton or twine.

clue.text: Delay the man's opening of international gallery?

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the Tate is a group of London art galleries

explanation.surface: A man postponing the launch of an international art show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' suggests a gallery launch but asks for a first letter. The Tate is Britain's national collection of modern and historic art, in London and elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To hesitate is to pause before acting, to hold back or put off, which is a form of stalling.

clue.text: Postpone visit

blocks.note: a court may suspend, or put off, an execution
a period spent somewhere, as in a hotel booking

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is legal: a stay of execution suspends a sentence. The second is the ordinary noun for a period spent somewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A court can suspend proceedings, and a holiday booking is a period spent at a place.
